title: 7. Why the Price Is What It Is: Valuation, Reverse DCF & Peer Comps

epigraph.quote: “Price is what you pay; value is what you get.”
epigraph.author: Warren Buffett

web_blocks.html: Start with the price, because the price is the question this chapter answers. The verified close on 12 November 2026 was ₹2,468.40, taken from the same-session market ledger. On 6.5 crore shares that is a market capitalisation of about ₹16,045 crore. Screener’s own card shows ₹15,928 crore at ₹2,466, so the two sources agree within about one percent. The trailing price-to-earnings multiple is 116x, and both Screener and TradingView show that figure. Every number in this chapter is measured against it, except the AZAD row of the peer table, which is the 13 November intraday row.

The price has already fallen a long way. The 52-week range runs from ₹1,360 to ₹3,128, and the stock sits 21% below its high. On trailing earnings of about ₹21 a share, the multiple was roughly 64x at the 52-week low and about 147x at the high. The market moved the multiple across a very wide band inside one year, which tells us how much of today’s valuation rests on sentiment rather than on reported profit.

The same-session snapshot does not carry a long-run multiple history, so this chapter makes no claim about an average. It asks instead what the current price assumes. Reverse DCF is the cleanest test. It asks which steady-state profit would justify today’s equity value at a required return. Using a 12% cost of equity and 5% long-run growth, the market value of ₹16,045 crore implies steady-state profit of about ₹1,123 crore a year. That is 8.4 times FY2026 net profit of ₹134 crore. At the FY2026 net margin of 22.2% (₹134 crore on ₹603 crore of sales), the same profit requires sales of roughly ₹5,054 crore, about 8.4 times the ₹603 crore reported for FY2026. This perpetuity test ignores the reinvestment that growth needs, so it understates what the price asks.

web_blocks.the_number: About ₹178 crore of annual net profit, at a 90x multiple, is what ₹16,045 crore of equity value requires.
web_blocks.how_calculated: Divide the market capitalisation by the chosen multiple. This is an earnings hurdle, not a discounted cash-flow value.
web_blocks.the_inputs: Market capitalisation of ₹16,045 crore at ₹2,468.40 on 6.5 crore shares; reference multiples of 60x (bear), 90x (base and bull) and 106x (the listed peer median).
web_blocks.the_range: At 60x the hurdle is about ₹267 crore; at 90x about ₹178 crore; at 106x about ₹151 crore.
web_blocks.if_off: Our base case of about ₹171 crore of FY2028 profit sits just below the 90x hurdle. The price therefore already assumes slightly more than our central case, and the margin of safety is negative on that basis.

web_blocks.html: Our earnings path rests on reported figures and disclosed guidance. H1 FY2027 net profit was ₹67.2 crore, up 6.6% [16]. Working back from FY2026 net profit of ₹134 crore gives a second-half FY2026 base of about ₹71 crore. Carrying that base forward at the same 6.6% gives second-half FY2027 profit of about ₹76 crore. FY2027 net profit therefore comes to about ₹143 crore, or ₹22 a share. The base case then assumes FY2028 profit rises 20% to about ₹171 crore, which is ₹26.4 a share. That is below the approximately 25% top-line growth the Q4 FY2026 call guided to for the current year [6], which the transcript does not date more precisely, and the gap is the point. Revenue rose 28.6% in the first half [22] while profit rose 6.6% [16], so the profit line is not keeping pace with the sales line.

web_blocks.takeaway: The bull case needs revenue to roughly double in two years. The base case needs profit to grow about 20% a year from FY2027 to FY2028, after about 13% a year from FY2026. The bear case is what happens if the cash cycle keeps absorbing the earnings.

web_blocks.takeaway: No listed Indian peer in the ledger is a pure-play turbine-airfoil supplier. The table is a sector cross-check on multiples, not a clean comparable.

web_blocks.html: The peers give a second check. The three names in the same-session snapshot trade at 122x (Bharat Forge), 87x (Astra Microwave) and 106x (BEML) trailing earnings, with a median of 106x. Bharat Forge is in Stage 4 and below its 30-week average, so its multiple reflects a falling chart as much as a fundamental view. Astra Microwave is in Stage 2 with a trailing operating margin of about 25%, but its trailing revenue growth is only 4%. BEML is in Stage 2 with a trailing operating margin of about 5% and revenue growth of 22%. AZAD’s trailing operating margin is 27% on TradingView’s definition and 37% on the audited-year basis used in Chapter 3. The gap is definitional and does not change the multiple the market pays.

We use 90x as the base multiple, about 15% below the peer median. The discount reflects two things the peers do not share. AZAD’s operating cash flow was negative in FY2026 and in the first half of FY2027 [17][23], and its earnings depend on a small number of long-cycle programmes. Chapter 9 shows what the answer becomes at other multiples, and why the verdict sits close to the hurdle.

What would move the valuation view. Raise the base multiple only if operating cash flow turns positive for a full year and profit growth returns to the 20% range. Lower it if second-half FY2027 profit growth stays in single digits, or if debtor days climb again beyond the FY2026 level of 189.

book_paragraphs: You and I have to start with the price, because the price is what we would be paying for the business. On 12 November the stock closed at ₹2,468.40. On 6.5 crore shares that is roughly ₹16,045 crore of equity, and the trailing multiple is 116 times earnings. That number is not a verdict. It is a question, and the question is what a buyer at this price has to believe.

Let us put the question in its plainest form. Ask what steady-state profit would justify the equity value at a reasonable required return. At 12% and 5% long-run growth, the answer is about ₹1,123 crore a year, which is 8.4 times the profit the company earned in FY2026. If the company earns at its current margin, that profit needs sales of about ₹5,054 crore. The company reported ₹603 crore for FY2026. The arithmetic does not say the business is impossible. It says the price is asking for a very large business that has not yet been built.

Now test the multiple. Our base case puts FY2028 profit at about ₹171 crore and applies 90 times, which gives ₹2,373 a share. The peers we can see trade at 87 to 122 times trailing earnings, so the market is not pricing AZAD as an outlier. We still take 15% off the peer median, because the company has consumed cash in the years it reported profits. That discount is a judgment, and you should hold us to it.

The second-half numbers matter more than any single year. First-half profit grew only 6.6% while revenue grew 28.6%. If that gap persists, the multiple has to carry the valuation, and multiples are the first thing to compress when a cyclical name misses its cash targets. The stock has already shown how wide that swing can be: the multiple was about 64 times at the 52-week low and about 147 times at the high on the same trailing earnings base.

What would change our mind is cash, not chatter. A year of positive operating cash flow, with profit growth back near 20%, would justify a higher base multiple. A second half in single-digit profit growth, or debtor days rising past 189, would justify a lower one. Until one of those things happens, you and I are paying for a business we can see clearly and a cash cycle we cannot yet trust.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: A high multiple is not a sin in itself. It is a promise that someone will keep earning more later. Our job in this chapter is to find out how much later, and how much more, before we decide whether that promise is worth paying for today.
